articles.title: Tennessee's Andrew Jackson estate spans 1,200 acres; its new plan puts much of a 70,000-square-foot visitor center underground so the building does not interrupt views across the historic landscape
articles.summary: US News: Plans for a $132 million redevelopment of The Hermitage, the 1,200 acre historic estate of former US President Andrew Jackson, will put much of a new .
articles.body: Plans for a $132 million redevelopment of The Hermitage, the 1,200 acre historic estate of former US President Andrew Jackson, will put much of a new 70,000 square foot visitor and education center underground to protect sightlines across the historic grounds. The Andrew Jackson Foundation announced the project, calling it a "generational transformation," to replace the current visitor facilities built in 1989. By placing large parts of the new complex underground, designers hope to keep views across the estate clear and help visitors feel like they've stepped back into the 19th century. Under the new site plan, called "Held by the Land," the redevelopment will change visitor paths, add a new tree-lined entrance, build an outdoor amphitheater, and restore historic spaces across the property, according to coverage by Nashville public radio station WPLN News.Reimagining the historic landscapeLocated near Nashville, Tennessee, The Hermitage is a major presidential historic site holding roughly 800,000 artifacts and historic items. Project organizers said the current facilities no longer meet the needs of daily operations or storage for the collection. Leaders of the Andrew Jackson Foundation approved the full master plan to shift the estate's focus toward its natural surroundings. Putting the main education complex underground keeps modern buildings from towering over the fields and historic outbuildings nearby. Jason Zajac, president and chief executive officer of the Andrew Jackson Foundation, spoke about the responsibility of managing the site in an official statement released alongside the announcement. "The Hermitage is more than a presidential home. It is a place where some of the most consequential and complicated chapters of American history unfolded," Zajac said. "We have an immense responsibility to preserve this place while making sure the story we tell reflects the full history of the people who lived, worked and were enslaved here, as well as the nation shaped during Jackson's lifetime and presidency."Funding and public supportThe total cost of the project is estimated at $132 million, with most of the money expected to come from private donations. Public support has already started at the state level. Tennessee state lawmakers approved $6 million in funding to begin planning and early design work, as reported by WPLN News. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee spoke in support of the project in a statement about the historic property's educational value. "The Hermitage is an important part of Tennessee's history and helps tell the story of our state and our nation," Lee said.Expanding site interpretation and historyThe physical redevelopment comes alongside ongoing efforts by the foundation to update how history is presented across the 1,200 acres. In recent months, site historians have been updating guided tours, including the "In Their Footsteps" program, which focuses on the lives of people enslaved on the plantation. As noted in earlier reporting by WPLN News, these updates aim to give a fuller picture of the enslaved men, women, and children who lived and worked at The Hermitage. The new visitor and education facility will include larger gallery spaces and research areas to better display artifacts and share these connected histories with the public. A timeline for building and finishing the new underground complex will be set as design work moves forward.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Sri Lankan court sentences 15 men to life in prison for roles in deadly 2019 Easter bombings
articles.summary: A Sri Lankan court convicted 15 men on Tuesday over their involvement in the 2019 Easter bombings that killed 267 people, and sentenced them each to at least 200 years in prison, meaning they will spend the rest of their lives behind bars.
articles.body: COLOMBO, Sri Lanka — A Sri Lankan court convicted 15 men on Tuesday over their involvement in the 2019 Easter bombings that killed 267 people, and sentenced them each to at least 200 years in prison, meaning they will spend the rest of their lives behind bars. The three-judge High Court panel also ordered the property of the defendants confiscated and any transfers invalidated under the South Asian country’s tough anti-terror law. The verdict was delivered amid tight security, with hundreds of police officers deployed around the courthouse, following a lengthy trial that spanned nearly five years. The April 21 attacks targeted three churches and three hotels across the island nation during Easter services and celebrations. They also wounded 574 people. The bombings, which were inspired by the Islamic State group, were among the deadliest attacks in Sri Lanka’s history. They killed 42 foreigners and devastated communities across the country. All the convicted men were from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community. Authorities filed 23,270 charges in 2021 against 25 suspects accused of planning or inspiring the attacks. One of them died pending trial. The charges included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism, and firearms and explosives offenses under the Prevention of Terrorism Act. None of those believed to have directly participated in the attacks are alive. Two Sri Lanka-based Islamic militant groups were accused of carrying out the bombings. In the courtroom, the accused appeared relaxed, chatting and laughing with each other during breaks. They even asked for and were granted a prayer break during the lengthy reading of the judgment. Nine defendants were freed after the court found that the charges against them were not proven. Those freed tearfully hugged the rest as they were separated from the convicts, who were later invited to argue for lenient sentences. Seven defendants had no attorney representing them and spoke for themselves. The first defendant, Mohamed Ibrahim Mohamed Naufer, who is an Islamic cleric, said he did not wish to make any request for religious reasons. “According to Islam, no religious leader should plead with (secular) authorities over any matter. Therefore, I do not wish to state anything,” Naufer said. Prosecutors said he had used his teachings to radicalize the other defendants. He was sentenced to 220 years in prison with hard labor. In total, five defendants were sentenced to 200 years each, five to 220 years, four to 240 years each and one to 260 years, based on their involvement in conspiring and aiding in the attacks. “What I did or didn’t do only God and I know,” said Mohamed Ibrahim Saadiq Abdulla. “In the end all people will be resurrected and God will judge everyone,” he said. He was given 240 years in prison with hard labor. In calculating the sentences, the court considered all seven blasts: three at churches, three at tourist hotels and one at a motel where an attacker killed himself and two others after aborting his plan to attack a fourth hotel. Haripriya Jayasundara, who led the prosecution, called for longer prison terms, saying the defendants were part of a well-planned attack carried out with the intention of killing Christian worshippers and tourists, which was proven by a video recording left behind by one of the suicide bombers. The video, recorded the day before the bombings, showed the attackers with their faces covered, armed with rifles and swords and pledging allegiance to the then-Islamic State leader Abu Bakhr al-Baghdadi to make Sri Lanka an Islamic nation and wage war toward that end. Jayasundara said Abdulla, the fourth defendant, had traveled to Turkey and crossed over to Syria and fought for the IS group. Sri Lanka’s Catholic Church has claimed, without providing evidence, that those identified so far as perpetrators are not the masterminds behind the bombings, and that there was a bigger conspiracy behind the attacks. A parliamentary committee found that police and intelligence officials failed to act on repeated intelligence warnings of the attacks. In July, a former police chief and a former senior defense ministry official were also sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings of possible attacks. Sri Lanka has not carried out executions since 1976, meaning death sentences typically result in life imprisonment. After the bombings, allegations emerged that the attackers had links to Sri Lanka’s state intelligence services. The country’s Defense Ministry denied any involvement. In February, police arrested Suresh Salley, a former intelligence chief and retired army major general, in connection with the bombings. The government has alleged that Salley, who remains in custody, had prior knowledge of the attacks and actively conspired to carry them out. Salley was a prominent military intelligence official credited with playing a major role in the campaign that ended the country’s civil war in 2009. The bombings shook the island nation and revived memories of the 26-year conflict with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, widely known as the Tamil Tigers, a separatist group that fought to establish an independent state for Sri Lanka’s ethnic Tamil minority.

articles.title: Migrants taken to Dover after more than 30 hours at sea
articles.summary: Protesters gathered in Gosport after initial reports the small boat would be brought further west.
articles.body:
A total of 51 migrants arrived in Dover on a small boat after spending more than 30 hours at sea.

The arrival at 00:30 BST came after protesters gathered in the Hampshire town of Gosport on Tuesday evening as it was initially believed this is where they would be brought ashore.

The boat left the Normandy coast on Monday morning and the French coastguard, which shadowed it, said the migrants were in "precarious conditions" and refused help as they were "determined to take all risks to reach" the UK.

British rescue boats were sent to collect those on board, who were then transferred to Border Security Command.

A government spokesperson said Border Security Command worked "around the clock to protect our border and will continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival".

The French coastguard said the migrants had been on the small boat for more than 33 hours.

The Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) said it was tasked by HM Coastguard with assisting those on board "out of concern for their safety and deteriorating health".

Migrants could later be seen disembarking in Dover wearing orange life jackets and carrying personal belongings.

About a dozen protesters were spotted in the area, with local police having blocked off a nearby road.

It was initially expected the migrants would be taken to the Portsmouth area after local MP Dame Caroline Dinenage said the Home Office had said this was "increasingly likely".

Hundreds of anti-migrant protesters, surrounded by police, gathered near Gosport marina on Tuesday evening after the initial reports.

A number of men wearing black, several with face coverings, were at the front of the crowd. Some were chanting "send them back".

Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary said six people were arrested after protesters "became hostile towards officers".

"They remain in custody at this time and our inquiries into these incidents continue," a spokesperson added.

Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, shared a YouTube livestream of the boat from the Channel.

Thomas – a long-term campaigner against migrants – organised recent protests in Portsmouth and Dover.

The migrant dinghy appeared to have set off from close to the village of Vierville-sur-Mer, west of Bayeux.

It is rare to see small boat crossings depart from so far west.

Earlier this month, a dinghy was met by lifeboats from the Isle of Wight having set off from the Cherbourg area, triggering protests in Portsmouth.

It is thought to have made one of the longest journeys of any small boat in the Channel. Officials said at the time they believed it was a one-off rather than a sign of new tactics.

On Monday, some 17,480 migrants had arrived in the UK after crossing the Channel by boat so far this year.

That total was 46% down from the same time last year.

The National Crime Agency recently said the reduction was down to law enforcement activity, though one expert said other factors, such as improving security in Syria, may also be behind the decline .

Many migrants come from some of the poorest and most chaotic parts of the world.

They almost always ask to claim asylum once they are picked up by the UK authorities.

On Tuesday, defence minister Luke Pollard insisted the UK's borders were secure after a migrant boat reached the Kent coast without being intercepted.

Five people were detained and passed to Border Security Command after the dinghy made it to shore at Folkestone on Monday - the first undetected landing for a year.

articles.title: 'Almost all agents' data stolen? Hackers claim they breached FBI jobs site, stole 2TB of data
articles.summary: US News: The FBI is investigating an apparent cyberattack on its job application website after the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed it stole more than 2 tera.
articles.body: The FBI is investigating an apparent cyberattack on its job application website after the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed it stole more than 2 terabytes of data containing sensitive personal information about thousands of FBI employees and job applicants.The bureau confirmed that it was investigating unauthorised activity affecting FBIjobs.gov, while the website’s Special Agent applicant portal was unavailable on Tuesday.ShinyHunters claimed on its dark-web site that it had obtained “very sensitive data” on almost all FBI agents and people who had applied for jobs with the bureau. The group also claimed it had accessed the FBI’s criminal justice, human resources and other systems.However, Axios said it could not independently verify whether the stolen data was legitimate or current. Cybersecurity researchers told the publication that the attack itself appeared legitimate, while 404 Media obtained a sample of the alleged stolen data that appeared to contain information on about 5,000 people identified as FBI agents.What hackers claim they stoleAccording to Axios, ShinyHunters said the data included names, agent status, email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses and, in some cases, information about spouses, including Social Security numbers.The group also claimed it used a zero-day vulnerability in Oracle’s PeopleSoft platform to access and deface the FBI’s jobs website. The site remained offline on Tuesday afternoon.Cybersecurity experts told Axios that the potential exposure could pose a long-term risk to FBI employees and their families if the information is circulated among other criminal groups or sold on the dark web.Allan Liska, a threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future, told Axios that the data was likely to be repeatedly downloaded and shared with other threat actors if it had been obtained as claimed.Andrew Brandt, principal threat intelligence incident commander at Huntress, said the biggest concern was whether ShinyHunters would sell the information to criminal or state-sponsored hackers.Why did ShinyHunters target the FBI?The group claimed the attack was not financially motivated. Instead, it demanded that the FBI retract or revise statements the bureau made about its activities.In a May advisory, the FBI warned that ShinyHunters commonly uses harassment tactics against victims and their families, including threatening calls and messages and, in some cases, swatting.ShinyHunters disputed the FBI’s description, telling Axios that other “low-skilled threat actors” had been carrying out attacks while using the group’s name.The FBI did not say whether it had confirmed the identity of the attackers or the extent of any data compromise.The incident comes as US law enforcement agencies face repeated cyberattacks. CNN reported that the FBI investigated a separate suspected breach in March involving a sensitive network used to manage wiretaps and intelligence surveillance warrants.Last month, hackers also leaked files they allegedly stole from the Justice Department’s Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. CNN reported that the material appeared to contain sensitive information from past investigations.The FBI has also faced cyber incidents in the past, including a 2023 breach of a computer system used by its New York field office for child sexual exploitation investigations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: China expands export controls on drug precursors ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
articles.summary: China said Tuesday that it is now requiring permits for exports to the United States, Mexico and Canada of two additional chemicals that can be used to make illegal drugs, expanding controls on shipments to the three countries.
articles.body: BEIJING — China said Tuesday that it is now requiring permits for exports to the United States, Mexico and Canada of two additional chemicals that can be used to make illegal drugs, expanding controls on shipments to the three countries. The Commerce Ministry and other authorities jointly announced the new regulations ahead of this week’s meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump. The additions bring the number of chemicals under such controls to 18. The U.S. has called China the world’s largest producer of many of the precursor chemicals used in the illicit production of fentanyl, methamphetamine and other deadly synthetic drugs. It has urged Beijing to take more aggressive action to reduce the flow of unregulated precursor chemicals. In November 2025, Beijing announced export restrictions on 13 “drug-making” chemicals to the U.S., Canada and Mexico, including chemicals used to produce the synthetic opioid blamed for tens of thousands of overdose deaths in the U.S. every year. In May, China added three additional types of fentanyl-related precursors to the list. The measures followed meetings between Xi and Trump in South Korea in October 2025 and Beijing in May. China faced a fentanyl-related tariff imposed by the U.S. Beijing then issued a report in March 2025 detailing its efforts to control the illegal trade in fentanyl. Its foreign minister also blasted the U.S. for responding to Beijing’s goodwill with tariffs. The U.S. Supreme Court struck down the tariff in February.

articles.title: A lot’s changed since Xi Jinping’s last US state visit. Mostly in China’s favor
articles.summary: When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visits Washington this week, he will be sitting down with President Donald Trump in a vastly different position than the last time the two men met face-to-face in the United States nearly a decade ago.
articles.body: When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visits Washington this week, he will be sitting down with President Donald Trump in a vastly different position than the last time the two men met face-to-face in the United States nearly a decade ago. At that 2017 summit at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort China was lagging America on multiple fronts and vulnerable to the tech and trade frictions Trump would unleash on it in the coming year. Now, Xi arrives at the helm of a country that’s transformed. The world’s second largest economy has emerged as a tech heavyweight. Home-grown tech talent is spurring Chinese AI models ever closer to Silicon Valley’s frontier. Beijing-based space firms are launching and landing reuseable rockets with their sights on global champion SpaceX. Companies from energy to AI, robots and memory chips have launched blockbuster stock debuts over the past year. China’s manufacturing juggernaut racked up a $1.2 trillion global trade surplus last year, due in part to surging demand for its electric vehicles, solar panels and chips. Its grip on the supply chains for some exports – especially rare earths – has given Beijing unique leverage over Washington and Trump’s “America First” trade war. And at a moment when the US is antagonizing allies and has yet to find a way to end its war on Iran that’s destabilizing the global economy, Xi has been burnishing China’s image as a responsible and dependable global leader. Throughout policy circles in Beijing, there is a consensus: gone are the days when the US could make one-directional demands of China. “China is far more confident than nine years ago and what’s even more important is that today China has found an effective way to keep the US in check,” said Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Shanghai’s Fudan University, who advises the government on foreign policy. “Washington has to treat Beijing with more equality, respect and this relationship has to be more and more reciprocal.” That doesn’t mean the stakes are low for Xi as he arrives in Washington for an expected three-day stay. The Chinese leader is banking on China’s high-tech transformation to inject momentum into a slowing economy. Maintaining “constructive strategic stability” – an ambition the two sides agreed to during a meeting in Beijing in May – could help ensure frictions or conflict with the US don’t get in the way. But buoyed by China’s growing global and technological clout, Xi will also be presenting to the US a new reality: while Beijing wants a stable relationship with the US, its rise doesn’t depend on it. In a bullish editorial in party mouthpiece the People’s Daily on Wednesday that helps illustrate this confidence, China’s ambassador to the US warned that Taiwan and human rights are “red lines” for Beijing that cannot be crossed. “China’s sovereignty, security, and development interests must not be violated. The four red lines concerning the Taiwan issue, democracy and human rights, China’s political system and development path, and its right to development must not be challenged,” Xie Feng wrote. Self-sufficient state For Xi, a key source of that confidence has been China’s ability to diversify trade away from the US market and build out its technological self-sufficiency – two mandates sharpened by pressures on China from the first Trump administration. Beijing has funneled vast financing and political will toward building its own technology in cutting-edge sectors – like robotics, AI, biotech, space, new energy and chips – and applying that tech into industry. The fruits of that growth, however, are not spread evenly. Youth unemployment hit a recent high last month. Hundreds of millions of workers rely on the gig economy, such as delivering food or driving ride-share cars for their primary work. Consumption lags, local governments struggle under debt and a huge property sector crisis rumbles on. People from all walks of life in China will readily tell you that the economy is just not doing as good as it used to be. But alongside this, there is often a sense of pride that the country has been able to rise as a tech power, even in the face of US-imposed restrictions. Look no further than the case of Huawei, the Chinese tech giant blacklisted by the first Trump administration. In recent days Chinese tech vloggers have been gleefully posting videos about Apple’s much-hyped release of its first foldable phone. They point out that Huawei’s own foldable model came out seven years ago. Days ahead of Xi’s visit to the US, Huawei also announced that its next generation of Ascend AI chips would be released ahead of schedule next year, signaling progress in what has been a crucial bottleneck for China in AI development. “We cannot accept a destiny where we cannot control our fate being determined by others in terms of willingness to sell chips to China or not,” Huawei rotating chairman Eric Xu said earlier this month. And while the American public is largely pessimistic about the development of AI, their peers in China are more focused on how it might impact their day-to-day lives. Job displacement is a concern, but there’s also a sense there is an opportunity to be seized – and that the ruling Communist Party, with its tight control over society, won’t let the technology spin out of control. ‘Equally matched’ Xi is heading to the US in the middle of an explosion of conversation about the risks of AI, including from Chinese models. Trump has said the country can’t slow development for safety, because it must focus on beating China. That puts the spotlight on a key aim from Xi and his delegation: to dissuade the US from more tech restrictions that further could limit Chinese firms’ access to American technology or markets. China wants to see “greater predictability in the economic and technology relationship” and a “stronger political commitment to prevent sensitive issues — especially Taiwan and technology restrictions — from destabilizing the overall relationship,” according to Sun Chenghao, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Center for International Security and Strategy in Beijing. But this is also where the shifting balance of power between China and the US comes in. Both sides know that new restrictions – if seen by Beijing as too aggressive – could reignite the conflict that led their economies to the brink of full decoupling last year. The truce that ended that round of their trade war was reached only after Beijing threatened a massive expansion of export controls on strategically critical rare earths, in response to a US move that would have vastly expanded the number of blacklisted Chinese firms. That truce will likely be extended this week – and both sides will be wary of pushing the other too far in a situation where “nobody wins, because it’s equally matched,” according to Kurt Tong, managing partner at The Asia Group advisory firm. “In the economic space, there isn’t really any superior player … because of the equally matched leverage aspects, the two sides are pulling back from actions that cost them to execute,” said Tong, who formerly served as the US consul general of Hong Kong. Now, Trump “looks at Xi Jinping and sees a counterpart as opposed to someone to wrestle into submission,” he said. Xi’s world China is now seen more positively than the US in most of 36 countries surveyed in a new Pew Research poll published in July. Xi even edged out Trump in winning people’s confidence, the pollsters found. These changes come not just alongside a shake-up of the role of the US on the global stage, but a shift in China’s ability to wield soft power. People around the world are using Chinese AI models for their businesses and driving Chinese EVs. Viral cultural exports like the Labubu plushy and Chinese dramas, as well as the online Chinamaxxing trend have driven interest and tourism in China. Xi has spent recent weeks on a rare series of overseas diplomatic junkets, sharing his own pitch for China’s leadership and worldview. At a summit of the BRICS group of emerging economies in New Delhi earlier this month, he pledged to help member states set up smart factories and develop AI models. During a state visit to Egypt earlier this month, Xi laid out proposals for a “new security architecture” in the Middle East – one that won’t be reliant on the US security umbrella. A host of leaders have also beat a path to Beijing’s door this year. The White House, meanwhile, in recent weeks has looked to point blame for the ongoing war it began in Iran on countries that continue to do business with its government, pledging to force them to stop or face major sanctions. As Iran’s biggest trade partner, China is at the top of that list. But here too is also an example of how China’s growing stature – and leverage – may come to bear in the upcoming talks. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Beijing last week. The talks in part were meant to “clarify some issues, so that in Washington, the two leaders can have more substantive discussion on this issue,” according to Wu, the policy advisor. That gives Beijing runway to signal that any move to censure its companies will see Washington lose any chance to benefit from China’s ability to speak to both sides. “China will tell the US two things,” Wu said. “One is – do not try to sanction Chinese banks or companies for doing business with Iran … secondly, forget about military solutions or economic sanctions (to end the conflict), you have to sit down to negotiate for a reasonable peace agreement.”

articles.title: Listening to loud music on a Singapore bus? It’ll cost you
articles.summary: Passengers who put their feet on seats, litter, or eat on public transit could be fined up to $390.
articles.body: Most bus passengers know how annoying it is when a fellow commuter blasts music or has a loud conversation on speakerphone. Now in Singapore, bus passengers could be fined hundreds of dollars for doing just that. It’s part of a crackdown on “disruptive” behavior on public buses in the Asian city-state, with fines of up to 5,000 Singapore dollars (SGD), or about $3,900, for those who break the rules. Passengers who cause “annoyance” to others by placing their feet on seats, playing audio at loud volumes, littering, eating or drinking on the bus could be fined up to 500 SGD ($390), according to a statement by the Land Transport Authority (LTA), which oversees public transit in Singapore. Serious offenses like causing danger to fellow commuters or “the soiling of any part” of a bus or other transit infrastructure carry a maximum penalty of 5,000 SGD. “Public transport is a shared space, and every commuter has a part to play in ensuring a gracious and pleasant commuting environment,” said the statement from the LTA. The new penalties align with pre-existing rules on Singapore’s subway system. Unlike major US cities like New York, transit systems in Asia are largely known for their cleanliness, order and efficiency, and bans on drinking, eating and playing music on board are common. In Japan, for example, even chatting with fellow commuters is considered rude. Singapore, known for its strict laws to enforce public cleanliness, is not alone in its efforts to create a more peaceful commute. The issue has become particularly pronounced in London, where last year authorities launched an etiquette campaign to urge passengers to use headphones while riding the tube. Around 70% of London transit users said they found it disruptive when commuters played loud music or spoke on the phone loudly without headphones — a practice some have nicknamed “bare beating” — according to a poll commissioned last year by Transport for London. Public transit operators in cities including Beijing, Kraków and Toronto have banned playing loud audio without headphones, though enforcement varies. While some disorderly commuters may walk away with a verbal warning, others have had to “face the music” for their annoying behavior. In February 2025, a man in France was fined $200 for taking a loud phone call on speaker while in a train station after he refused to turn the speaker off.

articles.title: Alibaba unveils what it calls China’s most powerful chip and ambitious AI model plans
articles.summary: China’s Alibaba unveiled new artificial intelligence chip technologies and plans for more powerful models on Tuesday, including what it said was China’s most powerful AI chip.
articles.body: HONG KONG — China’s Alibaba unveiled new artificial intelligence chip technologies and plans for more powerful models on Tuesday, including what it said was China’s most powerful AI chip, days ahead of a meeting between Chinese and U.S. leaders at which competition to lead on AI technology is expected to be a major theme. Alibaba’s announcement came as U.S. AI leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, are warning that China’s development of AI poses a threat to the United States and calling for an overall slowdown on development of the technology. Chinese leader Xi Jinping is set to arrive in Washington on Wednesday for a state visit and meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump, at which AI, trade and tariffs are expected to be discussed. At its annual flagship conference in Hangzhou, Alibaba rolled out a new AI chip and described its plans for the next generation of its AI model. CEO Eddie Wu said the new Zhenwu V900 chip is the “most powerful AI chip in China today” and can deliver three times the performance of the company’s previous generation Zhenwu M890 chip. Such chips power frontier AI model training and “inference,” a term for the calculations a trained AI uses to deliver responses to users. Alibaba’s Zhenwu chips are used in its data centers, providing computing to the company and its cloud clients. Alibaba also said it plans to train a new AI model at the scale of five to 10 trillion parameters, a measure of an AI’s learning capacity, bringing it closer to the most advanced models from the U.S. Its latest Qwen3.8-Max model, the most powerful of its Qwen AI series models, has 2.4 trillion parameters. Chinese AI company Moonshot says that its Kimi K3, released in July, is the world’s largest open model with 2.8 trillion parameters. Alibaba also highlighted plans to expand the data centers that power its cloud computing business, citing “exponentially” rising demand for AI computing. The company said it expects to have over 20 gigawatts’ worth of computing by 2032. SpaceX has approximately 1.4 gigawatts of AI computing capacity as of the middle of this year and says it aims to reach over 10 gigawatts in 2027. Recent Chinese advancements in AI are giving Beijing more leverage in its upcoming talks with Washington, some analysts believe, as China steps up its self-reliance push even as U.S.-led export restrictions have barred it from accessing some of the world’s most cutting-edge technologies, including AI chips and chipmaking machines. Open Chinese models, which are often more affordable than cutting-edge closed models from leading U.S. AI labs, have also been making inroads globally, including in the U.S. Chinese technology giant Huawei last week also unveiled new chip technologies as it looks to challenge global leaders like Nvidia. Frontier AI model training in China often relies on Nvidia chips, analysts said, but Chinese-designed chips are gaining ground as Nvidia has been blocked from selling some of its most powerful AI chips to China. “Using extra computing power to make up for chip limits helps China stay strong locally,” said Neil Shah, vice president of Counterpoint Research, a technology market research firm based in Hong Kong. Counterpoint senior analyst Parv Sharma added that how much the AI and chipmaking gap between China and the U.S. narrows will also depend on other factors including China’s ability to advance chip foundries that manufacture them, not just chip design capabilities. Alibaba is “mobilizing every resource” to meet customers’ demand for AI, CEO Wu said in his speech Tuesday. Global shortages across the AI data center supply chain, for example, “are currently limiting the speed at which we can scale our compute infrastructure” for AI, he added. Wu also likened AI growth to the industrial revolution and said “machine intelligence” will rapidly outgrow human thinking capacity. While “machine intelligence today is not a substitute for human intelligence,” he predicted that, eventually, machines will be able to produce over 1,000 times more “thinking” than all of humanity combined, up from less than 3% currently.

articles.title: Karnataka man murdered in Sharjah, body cut into 9 pieces; wife, son untraceable, says kin
articles.summary: UDUPI: A Kundapur man from Karnataka’s Udupi district was allegedly murdered in Sharjah in July, with his body later discovered in nine pieces, his br.
articles.body: UDUPI: A Kundapur man from Karnataka’s Udupi district was allegedly murdered in Sharjah in July, with his body later discovered in nine pieces, his brother told reporters on Tuesday.Alwin, who was working in the UAE, last contacted his family around July 20, his elder brother said on Tuesday. Messages were subsequently sent from Alwin's phone saying he was unwell and resting.The family became suspicious because Alwin usually communicated through voice notes and did not generally type messages, his brother said.“When we questioned him and asked him to make a call, there was no response after that,” the brother said.The family then contacted one of Alwin's classmates in Sharjah, who went to the apartment provided by his company. A watchman allegedly told the classmate that Alwin had left for India.The company's human resources department also initially told the family that he had travelled to India. But after the family said he had not arrived in India, his passport records were checked and he was reportedly found to still be in the UAE.A missing-person complaint was subsequently filed in Sharjah.Body found in carAccording to Alwin's brother, the body was found on August 12 inside the boot of Alwin's Toyota car, which had been abandoned on a road leading towards Oman.The family alleged that Alwin had been stabbed in the chest and that his body was cut into nine pieces before being packed into two bags.His identity was confirmed through DNA matching using a sample from his son, who works with Nestlé, the brother said.The family has received the death certificate but is yet to obtain a copy of the FIR, he said.'Unable to contact wife and son'Alwin had been married to Tina Kundar for around 20 years. The couple have a son who is currently studying in Class 10 in Dubai. Tina was working as a schoolteacher in Dubai, according to the family.The family said it has been unable to contact Tina and their son.They also claimed that CCTV footage from the apartment showed two men and a woman moving luggage. However, the family said it did not have definitive information on whether Tina had been questioned by UAE police.“We cannot say anything conclusively without the FIR copy. But reports indicate that they may have left for India around July 26 or 27,” the victim’s brother said.The family has approached Tina's native place along with her mother and is preparing to file complaints regarding the disappearance of Tina and her son.A complaint is also being lodged at Udupi Town police station, and the family has met the Udupi Superintendent of Police.The victim's brother said the family was seeking justice and demanded strict punishment for those responsible. He added that Alwin had not previously spoken of any marital or personal problems and had appeared normal when he visited his family in December.Udupi police yet to receive official confirmationUdupi district police said reports claiming that a person from Udupi was murdered in Sharjah were being circulated on local and social media platforms.However, police said they had so far not received any official information or confirmation from Sharjah Police or the Indian Embassy/Consulate in the UAE regarding the incident.Police said that if any official information is received, it will be verified and subsequently shared with the media.Stay updated with the latest Mangaluru news. articles.title: BMC proposes theatre tax hike; state nod awaited, old rates continue for now
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The BMC’s proposal to increase theatre tax on cinema halls and other entertainment venues is still awaiting approval from the state government.
articles.body: MUMBAI: The BMC’s proposal to increase theatre tax on cinema halls and other entertainment venues is still awaiting approval from the state government’s Urban Development (UD) Department, civic officials said. Until the revised rates are sanctioned and notified, only the existing rates will apply, officials said.The civic administration has proposed retaining the existing 2014-15 rates for 2027-28 until the state government approves the revised rates and issues a notification in the Official Gazette.The proposed revision, pending with the UD department, could see the tax on multiplex cinemas increase to Rs 400 per show from the existing Rs 60 for air-conditioned cinemas. The proposal provides for a tax of Rs 200 per show for single-screen AC cinemas, Rs 90 for non-AC cinemas, and Rs 100 per show for drama, jalsa and other entertainment programmes.Tajinder Tiwana, a law committee member, said the proposal was discussed in detail during the law committee meeting held on Tuesday and would be deliberated further.The BMC has been pursuing approval of the revised rates with the state government. According to the civic proposal, the revised rates will come into force only from the date specified by the state government in its Gazette notification.“For now, the old rates will continue to apply as the revised rates are yet to be sanctioned by the Urban Development Department,” a BMC official said.Under the existing rates, an AC cinema is charged Rs 60 per show and a non-AC cinema Rs 45 per show. Drama and other entertainment programmes attract Rs 25 per show, while circuses and funfairs are taxed at Rs 50 per day.The BMC has also proposed continuing the exemption from theatre tax for Marathi and Gujarati films, plays, one-act plays and tamashas, irrespective of the category of theatre.The 6% concession available since 1959 to taxpayers who pay their monthly theatre tax in advance by the fifth of the month is also proposed to continue for 2027-28.The annual theatre tax rates for 2027-28 will require approval from the Law Committee, Standing Committee and the Municipal Corporation.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: US, Iran hold mediated UNGA talks on ending war, opening Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Tehran ties diplomatic progress to lifting shipping blockades and unfreezing assets during New York negotiations.
articles.body:
The United States and Iran have engaged in hours of indirect talks through mediators on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, but accounts differed over whether officials from the two countries met directly.

US special envoy Steve Witkoff said mediators had “shuttled between” the American and Iranian delegations throughout Tuesday.

“Today, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, we engaged in lengthy talks with the Iranian delegation through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day,” Witkoff said in a post on X.

“They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising. The mediators will continue their work.”

US President Donald Trump gave a more direct account, saying Witkoff and Jared Kushner had held a three-hour meeting with Iranian officials.

“They had a very good meeting, a very productive meeting,” Trump told reporters at the UN, adding that he believed there was “a lot of momentum” towards an agreement. Trump later said talks were continuing and that he believed a settlement would eventually be reached.

Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett, reporting from Washington, said Trump’s initial comments had created confusion over who had participated. She said the White House later clarified that Trump had not attended and that Witkoff and Kushner represented the US side.

Al Jazeera’s Tohid Asadi, reporting from Tehran, said state media had confirmed a meeting between Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Witkoff after weeks without direct contact.

“This latest meeting was held at the request and insistence of the American side, and was aimed at conveying Iran’s messages and conditions, particularly around reopening the Strait of Hormuz,” Asadi reported.

Iranian state media said those conditions included lifting the US naval blockade, releasing frozen Iranian assets and ending the war on what Tehran describes as the “resistance” fronts.

Asadi also reported that an Iranian security source told Al Jazeera there could be room for further diplomatic engagement if Washington met Iran’s conditions and commitments.

The contacts came after a senior Iranian official told the Reuters news agency that Tehran’s delegation in New York had full authority to pursue diplomacy and described the UN gathering as a “golden opportunity” for Washington to return to negotiations.

The official said Iran had submitted its latest proposal to Washington through mediators on September 16 and that details of a possible agreement to end hostilities could be discussed in New York.

The official also said Iran could reopen Hormuz within seven days if the US eased military pressure and lifted its blockade of Iranian ports.

The indirect talks have been accompanied by a broader diplomatic effort involving the Gulf and other regional states.

Qatar said it was working with Pakistan to reduce tensions between Washington and Tehran, safeguard freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and promote regional stability.

Qatar’s Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani also met Araghchi in New York on Tuesday.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said they discussed developments in the region, efforts to de-escalate tensions and ways of creating conditions for dialogue.

Oman has also been involved in maritime diplomacy over the waterway, having previously discussed maritime arrangements with Tehran aimed at facilitating navigation through the strait.

Trump also met leaders and senior officials from Gulf Cooperation Council states, Turkiye, Jordan, Syria and Iraq on Tuesday to discuss Iran and regional security.

Reuters reported that a Qatari proposal for a common security framework involving Iran and Gulf states was among the issues under consideration, with one regional source saying Tehran was reviewing it.

The indirect talks came hours after Trump used his UNGA address to combine the possibility of an agreement with another warning of military escalation.

Trump said he faced a “big decision” between reaching a deal that would allow Iran to rebuild and moving to “annihilate the Islamic Republic”. He also said Washington had previously offered Tehran “full economic cooperation” in return for ending its nuclear programme and what the US describes as Iranian support for terrorism.

Iran’s General Staff of the Armed Forces and Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters responded in a statement carried by Iranian media, describing Trump’s threats as evidence of “strategic weakness” and saying Iran was ready to deliver “more severe, crushing, and unpredictable blows” in response to further attacks.

US officials have repeatedly suggested that negotiations were making progress following the collapse of the June memorandum of understanding. In early August, Trump said the sides had reached parameters for a possible agreement and later described talks over Hormuz as “moving along nicely”, although significant differences remained. Earlier this month, he again said he hoped the war was “towards the end”.

Tehran continues to condition the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz on the US easing military pressure and lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, while Witkoff said mediators would continue their efforts following Tuesday’s mediated exchanges.

articles.title: RAF Coningsby prepares for threats at home and abroad
articles.summary: Combat first-aid training and weapons drills are being stepped up at the station in Lincolnshire.
articles.body:
A front-line RAF base has expanded training for all personnel to reflect evolving threats at home and abroad.

RAF Coningsby, in Lincolnshire, is one of two quick reaction alert stations that protect UK airspace with combat-ready squadrons of Typhoon jets.

Military leaders have raised the level of force protection training, which includes combat first aid, additional firearms drills and awareness of chemical, nuclear and biological hazards.

Wing Cdr Ian Hart, who commands 29 Squadron, said the change in posture was "a recognition that the threat can come to us very, very easily in today's world".

He added: "We need to be ready here and we need to refresh those drills and be ready to act on them should any of those threats actually become a reality for us."

The base is the first in the UK to introduce Module 2 Individual Readiness Training as its minimum standard.

Hart said: "When we look at the unstable world and the threats we're facing, I think it just brings it home that actually we need to be ready wherever we are, all of the time."

He explained how combat first aid training reflected threats such as drone strikes.

"We've just finished our first aid training and when we talk about drones, if you look at what's going on in the Ukraine-Russia conflict, you see a lot of situations where you might be first on the scene, wherever you are.

"That could be at Coningsby, it could be overseas."

The enhanced training is delivered by the Force Protection Training Flight, a specialist team staffed by members of the RAF Regiment.

They are described by the service as "the unsung guardians".

Warrant Officer Lee Hargreaves, who commands the flight, said the training was mandatory for all personnel, "from pilots through to chefs, HR specialists through to musicians".

"Although they have a trade and a primary role to do, they still have to know the force protection skills so they can meet the requirement.

"Pilots make up about 4% of the Royal Air Force. The other 96% is what makes that 4% happen."

While RAF policy requires all personnel to hold Module 1 training as a minimum, Coningsby is the first RAF station in the UK to adopt Module 2 as standard.

The approach is being rolled out more widely across the service.

articles.title: Stafford teen lands role of Nia on Thomas the Tank Engine show
articles.summary: Ellie-Mae Siame, 14, says she was "in shock" but excited at being a part of the beloved series.
articles.body:
Earlier this year, young actor Ellie-Mae Siame landed a role in a show about one of the world's most recognisable characters – Thomas the Tank Engine.

The 14-year-old is the voice of Nia, the orange and black-coloured engine number 18 in Thomas & Friends: Railway Stories.

A full-length YouTube special premiered on Thursday, which has already been viewed more than two million times, and it will be on Netflix from 30 September before a full series airs in 2027.

"It was crazy to see how big Thomas the Tank Engine was – I knew it was big but not that big," Ellie-Mae told BBC Radio Stoke.

The Stafford teenager said she was contacted by her agent and did a filmed audition for the show in January.

She expected either not to hear back or be contacted to do a recall or a read-through – instead, she was offered the role of Nia straight away.

Ellie-Mae said: "It's crazy to think they liked my voice that much and gave me the opportunity to be Nia that fast."

"When I found out I got Thomas the Tank Engine, it was a shock but it was also really exciting," she added.

"It's opened such a big pathway – the doors to more opportunities and experiences."

Ellie-Mae has been acting since she was five years old, first appearing as Maudie in the 2020 film Four Kids and It.

Her credits since then have included Generation Z, His Dark Materials, Modern Love and My Week with Maisy, in which she starred alongside Dame Joanna Lumley.

The teenager said she loved both screen and voice acting, but added: "I think voice acting is probably my favourite because I don't have to learn a script.

"You get to change your voice a bit so it doesn't have to be your natural or your normal voice."

Initially, she did not realise how big a deal Thomas the Tank Engine was because she was "more into princesses" than trains.

But her parents' excitement, along with many others, showed her how beloved the franchise had become since it first arrived on TV screens in the 1980s, and in books for 40 years before that .

Ellie-Mae found the role particularly special as it meant combining her love of acting and singing – she can be heard on the programme's theme tune, for example.

She described recording one of the songs for an episode as being one of her favourite memories, along with seeing Nia on screen for the first time.

"I don't even know how to put it into words," she said. "It's such a big thing. Seeing how many people like Thomas the Tank Engine is crazy because I get to be a part of that.

"I don't know how to explain it, it's such an exciting part of my life and definitely something I'll remember forever."

articles.title: Turning a hobby into a business idea and making it pay
articles.summary: People in Devon and Cornwall describe finding satisfaction and a salary from their passion projects.
articles.body:
There is an old saying: "Find a job you love and you will never have to work a day in your life."

That for many people might prompt a snort of derision. But what if you could turn your favourite hobby into something that actually turned a profit.

The disruption caused by the Covid-19 pandemic and the opportunities of online retailing have opened up an entire world of serious side-hustles and enterprises on internet marketplaces.

The BBC has been to meet three people who gave up the day job to focus on making their passion projects pay.

Jackie Bird spent all her working life in the corporate world, where she had her own award-winning business redesigning office spaces in London.

This worked wonders until the pandemic and lockdown, when offices emptied and it seemed everybody worked from home.

Once the pandemic was over, returning to her line of work meant a 600-mile (966km) round trip from her home in Polperro, Cornwall, to London, which she said was "killing me".

"In April 2025, I decided to hang up my tool bag and follow my passion," Bird said.

"I sketch on to a canvas the outline of an image, and I can do that from people's photographs, and recreate them in ribbon form.

"It's quite abstract, like a pop art-type style , but using the medium of ribbon instead of paint.

"I did a few during the pandemic, but all I've been doing [recently] is commission after commission. I haven't really stopped in the last year.

"It's just amazing, I couldn't have wished for more. I didn't know this was going to be my outlet."

Tobias Kaye cheerfully admitted he struggled to find his path in life.

He said: "I seemed so lost as a teenager. I couldn't see how I was going to work in

"this world, it just seemed mad to me and, the more jobs I did, the more difficult I found it."

Kaye, who now lives in Buckfastleigh, Devon, got into woodturning after working with a relative, and settled down to make hundreds and hundred of wooden bowls.

But the breakthrough moment was when he realised he did not need to add an extra string to his bow - but rather add strings to his bowls.

"One evening I was meditating on the side of my bed and this image of a string stretched inside a bowl appeared in front of me.

"Since then, I have felt guided... of having the vision and ideas to produce these instruments."

Kaye named the instruments Sounding Bowls and they are now sold for use in therapy to the NHS and hospitals all over the world.

He had even trained other makers to cope with the demand, he said, claiming: "They are unique in the history of world music.

"It has strings inside a circular wooden space with no sound board on the top.

"So, unlike a violin or a guitar, which is a box instrument, this is an open resonator, and the thinness of the wood, thinner on the bottom than a matchstick, and really strong on the outside to take 20 strings, it gives the sound."

Will Pearson was running a screen-printing workshop in Falmouth, Cornwall, when the Covid pandemic hit, leaving his business "decimated".

Pearson remembered: "I went down the beach, I was in a blind panic. I took my boomerang with me and then I had an idea about manufacturing them.

"I've always had a pipe dream to start a boomerang brand, to make my own boomerangs and try to sell them, because boomeranging is a lot of fun. I started when I was nine."

"I've always enjoyed it, when I get my boomerang out people are always intrigued by it and I thought: 'Maybe there's something here. Maybe we could rekindle an interest in it,' and that's what we're trying to do."

Pearson has now opened up a boomerang shop in Falmouth, using his screen-printing skills to create T-shirts and to add a 1960s West Coast surf vibe.

"What takes a lot of my time is I am out in the field test flying boomerangs," said Will.

"I test fly every single boomerang to make sure it gives a complete return - if you've flown it right."

articles.title: Oompa Loompa actor Rusty Goffe retires after Netflix Wonka return
articles.summary: Rusty Goffe on working with his son and an AI-generated Gene Wilder in a new Willy Wonka TV show.
articles.body:
An original Oompa Loompa actor from the 1971 film Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory has retired after reprising the role one final time.

Rusty Goffe began his film career in the Gene Wilder movie, before later appearing in the original Star Wars, the Harry Potter films and Doctor Who.

Last year, Netflix flew the 77-year-old from his home in Leighton Buzzard, Bedfordshire, to Brisbane, Australia, where he once again donned a green wig and overalls for the TV competition Wonka's The Golden Ticket.

He said: "I started on Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory, and now Wonka's The Golden Ticket is my swan song. I've just ended my career on Willy Wonka. Isn't that wonderful?"

The 1971 film was the first screen adaptation of the 1964 novel Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, written by Roald Dahl at his home in Great Missenden, Buckinghamshire.

It followed Charlie Bucket, a child who is one of five winners who find "golden tickets" inside a Wonka bar and are invited to tour the mysterious chocolate factory run by the eccentric Willy Wonka.

Filmed mainly in Munich, Germany, it featured 10 actors of restricted growth who played the Oompa Loompas - the factory's workers.

Netflix bought the rights to Dahl's children's books from the author's family in 2021. Its new competition series sees 12 pairs of contestants compete for a cash prize inside a chocolate factory inspired by the original film.

Johnny Depp played Wonka in director Tim Burton's 2005 version of the story , while Timothée Chalamet played him in 2023's "origin" movie , directed by Paul King.

Goffe said returning to the world of Wonka more than half a century later felt "very surreal", although some things had changed.

He said: "Fifty-five years ago, the costumer thought every little guy had the same size head with the same size wigs, so they pull it on, rake it on, glue it, whatever to make it stay on.

"This time, they done their homework and the wigs were handmade, fitted just like a hat."

There were other improvements too. The orange make-up could now be washed off with soap and water, the shoes were more comfortable and the chocolate river was no longer full of cigarette ends discarded by crew members.

Goffe is not the only member of the original cast to feature in the series. Willy Wonka actor Gene Wilder "narrates" the show, explaining the various games to contestants.

The actor died in 2016, but his voice has been recreated using AI, which has received some criticism , despite producers obtaining the consent of his estate and approval of his widow Karen B Wilder.

Goffe described hearing his former co-star's voice on set as "magical".

"I thought, sometimes, he was on the set behind me," he said.

"It was perfect, because he is Willy Wonka, he really is. Working with him was excellent. He was a lovely guy. Nice, kind, funny. He was brilliant.

"Gene Wilder is Willy Wonka. There's no other person that could do it."

The other Oompa Loompas on the Netflix set were new to the production and included performers of different genders and heights.

Among them was his son, Ben Goffe, who has performed in Shakespeare in London's West End and has been working on a major film project in Spain.

Having grown up watching the 1971 classic on video and DVD, Ben jumped at the opportunity to travel to Brisbane and perform alongside his father.

Rusty described watching his son step on to the set in full costume as an emotional moment.

He said: "I was so proud to have him next to me in Willy Wonka... my hero was with me."

Despite appearing in many iconic films across his career, Rusty insists that none of them compare and "Wonka is magical".

He continues to attend conventions around the world to meet fans of the original film.

He said: "I've had a great career, the majority of it has been Willy Wonka."

When asked directly if this series was his final bow, he laughed: "I think so, unless someone offers me a few bob to go back and do something else."

Wonka's The Golden Ticket premieres on Netflix this week, with a two-part finale scheduled for 30 September.

articles.title: Man's body found in a river in Hertfordshire sparks IOPC inquiry
articles.summary: Police say they were chasing the man on foot in Stanstead Abbots in connection with two robberies.
articles.body:
The death of a man who was being chased by police before he was found in the River Lea, is being investigated by an independent watchdog.

Emergency services were called to the High Street and towpath in Stanstead Abbotts, Hertfordshire, on 14 September at about 13:20 BST.

Officers said they pursued the man on foot after identifying him as being wanted in connection with two robberies. He was no longer in their line of sight when he entered the water.

Hertfordshire Constabulary said it had referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which subsequently decided to launch an investigation.

"We are assisting the IOPC with its enquiries, and it would be inappropriate to comment further at this time", a police spokesperson said.

An IOPC spokesperson said officers had attempted to stop the man on the High Street. The man was later found in the river and pronounced dead at the scene.

The spokesperson added the investigation was in its "early stages" and that the man's family would be kept updated on its progress.

articles.title: New Hampshire man returns a magazine 132 years late after library introduces fine freeze, avoiding a potential $12,055 fine
articles.summary: US News: An overdue library magazine has returned to its original home in New Hampshire after more than 132 years. John Hanson, an 84-year-old man from Barring.
articles.body: An overdue library magazine has returned to its original home in New Hampshire after more than 132 years. John Hanson, an 84-year-old man from Barrington, recently brought a September 1894 issue of The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine back to the Concord Public Library. The publication had remained in his home for decades, although he said he had no idea how it came into his possession. His decision to return it followed the library's introduction of a year-long fine freeze in September 2026. The initiative allowed him to avoid a potential $12,055 late fee, calculated from 48,220 overdue days. The unusual return surprised library staff and raised questions about the magazine's journey through more than a century of history.New Hampshire man discovers 1894 magazine in his homeHanson, a Concord native, had kept the magazine at home for decades. According to New Hampshire Public Radio, the item was initially in his Boscawen home before he moved to Barrington in 2010. He said he had no clear recollection of how it came into his possession. His father was born and raised in Concord but did not have a library card, leaving the original borrower's identity uncertain. Hanson speculated that he might have acquired it through a book pile or an advertisement sale.Fine freeze encouraged overdue returnsThe Concord Public Library introduced a fine freeze on September 1, 2026, to encourage patrons to return overdue materials without accumulating additional penalties. The programme was announced as a year-long initiative to examine the effects of operating as a fine-free library. Hanson learned about the policy through a newspaper article and decided it was an appropriate time to return the magazine.The library said the magazine was 48,220 days overdue. At a theoretical rate of 25 cents per day, the resulting fine would have amounted to $12,055. However, Hanson did not have to pay the amount because of the fine freeze.The magazine dates back to September 1894The returned publication was an issue of The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine, a periodical that combined literature, history and current affairs. The magazine included period advertisements and material reflecting social concerns of the late 19th century. The Guardian reported that the issue also contained writings associated with authors such as Mark Twain and Henry James.The magazine's original library markings included a bookplate and an instruction stating that it could be kept for one week. Its long absence has left library staff curious about the identity of the original borrower and the circumstances that led to its disappearance.Library plans to preserve the historic returnThe Concord Public Library does not plan to place the 1894 magazine back into regular circulation. Instead, staff said the issue could be preserved as part of the library’s historical collection or displayed in the Concord Room, where archival materials related to the city are kept. Its age, condition and connection to the library’s own history make it more than an ordinary overdue publication. After spending decades in private hands, the magazine could now serve as a physical record of the library’s past and of an era when such periodicals were routinely borrowed, read and returned. Its preservation would also allow future visitors to examine a publication that has survived for more than 130 years and has now returned to the institution that originally owned it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump's 'annihilation' threat
articles.summary: The talks are the first since a ceasefire collapsed in June, with the sides exchanging fire intermittently.
articles.body:
Top Iranian and US officials have held talks at the UN in New York on a day when the US leader said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved.

No breakthrough has been reported from the meeting mediated by Qatar and involving Iran's foreign minister and US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff - the first since a June ceasefire unravelled.

Witkoff said a round of discussions had been completed "that we hope will prove constructive and promising". Iran repeated its demand for the US to end its "acts of aggression".

The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.

Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of prices.

It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November.

In his address at the annual meeting of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Trump began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime - remarks that sounded more pitched to voters the US midterms than the diplomats in the hall.

He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran - a huge contrast with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples.

The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise.

"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.

"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"

Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.

The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open.

Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly.

Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met Witkoff.

Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, quoted by state broadcaster IRNA, later said negotiations took part through a Qatari mediator who communicated Tehran's conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and to US "acts of aggression".

The BBC asked Witkoff how the meetings had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up. Witkoff later confirmed on X that the talks had been held "through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day".

"They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising," Witkoff said. "The mediators will continue their work."

Since the ceasefire collapsed, both sides have intermittently exchanged fire.

Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation.

The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast.

The US has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing a huge disruption to the Iranian economy.

In an effort to force Tehran to agree a deal to end the conflict, President Trump has also threatened sanctions against any country that continues trading with Iran. But so far, there has been no indication of a change of course in Iran, which insists the US and Israel end their war, including against the Iran-backed Shia group Hezbollah in Lebanon which Israel has been attacking.

Yemen's Houthis - also allied to Iran - have recently intesified attacks aimed at disrupting oil shipping from Saudi Arabia, promting an escalation of the conflict with the kingdom.

articles.title: Farmers offering on-site vacation rentals to combat rising costs
articles.summary: As farmers face rising operation costs, many are looking for additional ways to bring in more money and some are offering overnight stays on their properties in effort to do that.
articles.body: As farmers across the country face rising costs, some are turning to tourism to bring in money beyond their traditional agricultural operations. At Lynette Ralph's horse ranch in Missouri, vacationers can spend the night in a small cabin, wake up to views of the horses and get a firsthand look at ranch life. Guests can explore the property, pet and feed the horses or pay extra for horsemanship and riding lessons. "You have access to the farm life, the horses, the barns," Ralph said. THE $1,600 LETTUCE: CALIFORNIA GROWERS WARN OF ‘MASTER PLAN’ STRANGLING FAMILY FARMS For Ralph, welcoming guests is about more than offering a unique getaway. The income from offering short-term vacation rentals on site has allowed her to keep her ranch operating. "If I didn't have the short-term rentals associated with the riding program, I would have to probably liquidate, sell the horses, sell the property," she said. Airbnb and American Farmland Trust are launching a new grant program to help farmers earn extra income through tourism, the organizations told Fox News exclusively. According to USDA data cited in Airbnb's report, households associated with intermediate farms, a category of smaller operations where farming is the principal operator's primary occupation, reported a median loss of approximately $2,800 from farming in 2024. AMERICAN FARMERS PINCHED BY HIGH DIESEL PRICES AHEAD OF SPRING PLANTING SEASON David Haight, vice president of programs at American Farmland Trust, a national nonprofit dedicated to protecting farmland and supporting farmers, said finding additional sources of income could help some farm families navigate financial challenges. "Many families are looking for ways to diversify income, and so bringing people out to the farm or ranch for some is a way to help bring in other dollars," Haight said. Demand for farm stays is growing, according to Airbnb, which reported that online searches increased 61% during the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year. The company says the typical farm stay host earned approximately $8,000 in 2025, while U.S. farm stay hosts collectively earned nearly $120 million. Those figures represent hosting earnings, not necessarily profits after expenses. In Georgia, farm stay host Gilda Lyon said income from her existing rentals has allowed her to build additional cabins and invest in her farm. The money helped her build a greenhouse, start selling herbs and maintain blueberry plants. "The extra income actually has allowed me to invest, in many improvements and to expand the opportunities available for guests," Lyon said. AMERICANS CHOOSING TO VISIT SMALLER TOWNS OVER BIG CITIES AS TRAVEL COSTS RISE Airbnb and American Farmland Trust's new "Farm to Stay" Grant Program will award approximately 25 to 30 grants of up to $10,000 each, with applications opening in November. Haight said the grants may not cover every expense associated with welcoming visitors, but could help farmers in other ways, such as assisting in renovating barns for events, installing fencing or preparing accommodations for overnight guests. The benefits could also extend beyond individual farms. Haight said visitors may spend money at nearby restaurants, shops and other businesses, bringing additional tourism dollars into rural communities.
